newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: HONG KONG RETURNS TO CHINESE RULE
After 156 years of British rule, Hong Kong has been returned to Chinese rule.
The British handed the Territory back to the People's Republic of China in a simple midnight ceremony.
In the newly created special Administrative region of Hong Kong, the Chinese President, Jiang Zemin, pledged to uphold Hong Kong's social and economic ways of life.
President Jiang and Prince Charles watched as the Union Jack was lowered and the PRC's flag was raised.
GOVERNMENT WILL BY-PASS SENATE WITH CES REFORMS
Federal Employment minister Amanda Vanstone says the Government will bypass the Senate, to implement reforms to the Commonwealth Employment Service.

So far, the Senate has amended the Government's Employment Sevices Bill to ensure all jobseekers have access to the new corporatised CES and private sector job agencies, with public service conditions for CES staff.
Senator Vanstone says the Senate has delayed the Bill until August, which is unacceptable, so the Government will proceed with its reforms under existing legislation.
Senator Vanstone says she's investigating options to implement some changes earlier than previously announced, but the full package is likely to be delayed from March to May next year.
MURDER-SUICIDE MYSTERY
Tasmanian police say the reason for the Shoobridge family killings may never be known.
Police are continuing their investigations into the actions of Peter Shoobridge, who killed his four daughters and then himself at his house near Cambridge at the weekend.
They've examined more letters written by Shoobridge.
In one of them he talks about his funeral arrangements, but police won't reveal further details.
Detective Sergeant Tony Bennett says the letters will be examined by forensic and hand writing specialists in the hope of establishing a time-frame of the deaths.
He says police have no indication of the time span between when Shoobridge committed the crimes and wrote the letters, because there are no dates on them.
NATIVE TITLE CLAIM IN ALICE SPRINGS
The Federal Court will begin hearing a native title application over parts of Alice Springs today.
The month-long hearing has been scheduled, after the Northern Territory Government and the Aboriginal claimants failed to reach a negotiated outcome.
The Mbantarinya Arrernte claimants are seeking to prove their traditional links to Alice Springs - and therefore their native title - have survived European occupation.
Their claim covers crown land within Alice Springs, including the town's borefield.
If native title is proved, the claimants will seek the right to negotiate over future land uses within the town.
CHILD CARE FEES RISING AND CENTRES CLOSING SAY UNIONS
Unions say the latest surveys reveal government policy on community child care is causing fee increases and significant closures.
A national day of action, in all states today, will protest against the withdrawal of government subsidies for community child care.
ACTU Assistant Secretary, Greg Combet, says from today centres will struggle to survive.
Mr Combet says the AC of surveys in Queensland and Victoria, and of community based centres generally.
He says the surveys show increases in child care fees, reductions in staff at centres and compromises to quality.
He says that means the objectives of affordable and quality child care are being compromised by the government's cuts.
RECORD PRICE FOR ABORIGINAL PAINTING
An Aboriginal painting, stored in a Richmond shed for 25 years, fetched a record price at auction in Melbourne last night.
The painting was among works from five major collections offered by Sotheby's.
Water Dreaming at Kalipinya an early western desert painting by Johnny Warangula Tjupirrula was bought by an unamed buyer for $206,000.
Two works by Shorty Lungkarda Tjungarrayi sold for more than $100,000 each.
Sotheby's Aboriginal art expert Tim Klingarden says while there was keen bidding from overseas, 80 per cent of the works will stay in Australia.
STRESS LESS DAY
Psychiatrists in New South Wales will today advise people to think about what's worrying them - and then stop worrying about it.
It's Stress Less Day, which the New South Wales Association for Mental Health has named today after the crescendo of pressure marking the end of the financial year.
Spokesman Dr Nick O'Connor advises people to do less today and even o take an early mark from work.
And he has some suggestions on how to relax.
He suggests walking through grass or trying to win lotto today.
Dr O'Connor also suggests lifestyle changes such as learning how to do simple relaxation exercise or meditation and taking better care of our diet and the way we look after our bodies.
